title: WSO2 rebrands as Choreo Labs | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 18 November 2026 00:04
-     - {{hitsCtrl.values.hits}}

WSO2, the open source company whose software processes an estimated 60 trillion transactions a year and manages 2.5 billion identities, has announced it has a new name, Choreo Labs. 

The Company said enterprises are moving AI agents out of pilots and into production, and need to govern every one of those agents across the APIs, systems, and identities it touches, effectively choreographing each agent’s journey. As that happens, the company’s platform has moved beyond connecting enterprise systems to sitting at the centre in empowering enterprises to meet this demand for AI governance. The new name reflects that evolving role.

Founded in 2005, WSO2 took its name in the web services era. Today, its API management, integration, and identity products run in production for more than 950 customers in 90-plus countries, including banks, governments, hospitals, and telcos. The world’s leading analyst firms have recognised the company for its comprehensive product offerings and success in meeting enterprise customers’ demands. Over those two decades, enterprise software has moved from web services to cloud, APIs, and now AI agents that act on their own, and the company has moved with it.

Through each of those shifts, the company’s mission has stayed the same: connecting systems and controlling what moves between them. AI agents raise the stakes. 

Choreo Labs CEO Harry Ault said: “For over 2 decades, our mission has been to make sure enterprise systems talk to each other safely at scale. AI agents don’t change that mission. In fact, they make it far more urgent. Enterprises won’t put agents into production until they can see, govern, and trust every action those agents take. That is the problem we were built to solve, and our new name says so.”

“WSO2 was the right name for the company we started in 2005,” Ault added. “We’ve grown a lot since then, and so have the problems our customers bring us. Choreo Labs reflects the company we are today, and the principles we’ve always built on.” 

“Choreo” comes from choreography. Inside every enterprise, agents, APIs, integrations, identities, and services each have their own part to play, and none of them ever stops moving. Choreo Labs gives organisations both the freedom for each part to move and the control to keep them in step. Choreo, the company’s platform, brings APIs, integration, identity, agents, and the internal developer platform that runs them together in one place.

“Labs” reflects the company’s research and engineering culture. It has long innovated in open source and open standards, from its integration programming language to its latest agent management product. Technical staff make up more than 75% of its 850-plus employees, and the same engineers who design the platform work alongside customers to deploy it.

title: LAUGFS cuts gas prices | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 18 November 2026 00:03
-     - 81

LAUGFS Gas PLC yesterday said it has cut the price of its 12.5 kg domestic LPG cylinder by Rs. 745 to Rs. 5,995. The cut took effect from midnight yesterday, four days after the company raised its prices.

The price of the 5 kg domestic cylinder came down by Rs. 322 to Rs. 2,398. The company said the reduction also took account of the difficulties consumers face.

The cut still leaves prices above where they were before the increase, which took effect from midnight on 13 November, 2026. At the new prices, the 12.5 kg cylinder costs Rs. 1,030 more than before the hike and the 5 kg cylinder Rs. 410 more.

“Although the company will continue to incur losses at the revised price, the management of LAUGFS Gas PLC has decided to absorb these losses, considering the request made by [portfolio] Minister Wasantha Samarasinghe on behalf of consumers, while prioritising consumer relief despite prevailing financial challenges,” the company said.

The company had held its prices steady for a quarter before the increase, even as its input costs rose. Saudi Aramco’s monthly contract prices are the benchmark for most LPG imported into Asia.

“Despite rising import costs, including Saudi Aramco contract prices and freight charges due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, LAUGFS Gas PLC absorbed these additional costs without revising prices for three consecutive months,” the company said.

“However, sustained financial losses subsequently compelled the company to increase the price of a 12.5 kg LPG cylinder by Rs. 1,775,” it added.

Consumers can get district-wise prices and check product availability through the LAUGFS Gas hotline on 1345.

title: Hayleys backs Sri Lanka Expo 2027 as Gold sponsor, opening a path to global markets for Sri Lankan SMEs | Daily FT

Wednesday, 18 November 2026 00:01

Hayleys PLC receives partner recognition for Sri Lanka Expo 2027 at the Partnership Appreciation 

ceremony in Colombo

Hayleys PLC has joined Sri Lanka Expo 2027 as a Gold Partner. The Sri Lanka Export Development Board (EDB) will host the international trade exhibition from 14 to 17 January 2027 at the BMICH, Colombo, which returns after 15 years.

The Expo is expected to bring together about 750 Sri Lankan exporters and over 1,500 international buyers, investors and trade delegates. It covers sectors ranging from apparel, rubber and engineering to tea, spices, coconut products, ICT and logistics. 

In September 2026, the country’s merchandise exports reached $ 1.38 billion, the highest monthly value on record. Total exports for the first nine months of the year rose 5% to $ 13.6 billion.

Hayleys is Sri Lanka’s number one ranked listed company (LMD 100 – 2025/26) and is one of the country’s largest export earners. The Group accounts for around 5% of the country’s export income, close to $ 800 million in foreign exchange. It operates in more than 20 countries and its products reach over 80 markets.

Its export strength is built on value addition across the Group. Hayleys exports gloves, activated carbon, coconut fibre-based eco solutions products, textiles, aluminium extrusions, agricultural products and Ceylon tea. Its transportation and logistics businesses help keep the country’s trade moving as a facilitator for country’s exports. Each of these businesses competes on technology, research and quality in demanding international markets.

“Growing exports is a key pillar of Sri Lanka’s economic future, and it has been at the heart of Hayleys’ strategy,” said Hayleys PLC Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Mohan Pandithage. “Our growth and the nation’s growth rest on Sri Lankan products competing, and winning, in global markets. At the Expo, we are proud to feature Hayleys’ own sustainable innovations, home-grown solutions that have already won over customers in over 80 markets.”

The Group’s purpose is “to inspire an inclusive world and a thriving planet”, and that purpose shapes how it builds export value. Hayleys businesses bring smallholder farmers, out-growers and rural communities directly into global value chains, so they share in the value created. This work is driven by Hayleys Lifecode, the Group’s ESG and sustainability framework. Hayleys companies have together been named Sri Lanka’s Best Corporate Citizen six times by the Ceylon Chamber of Commerce.

Through its sponsorship, Hayleys aims to help Sri Lanka’s small and medium enterprises compete on the international stage the Expo provides.

“Sri Lanka’s SMEs are the next link in that chain. As Gold Sponsor of Expo 2027, we want to help local entrepreneurs do what Hayleys has done for generations: adopt sustainable practices, showcase their innovative products, and grow their portfolio to reach global markets. When they grow, Sri Lanka’s export base grows with them,” said Hayleys PLC Group Executive Director Sarath Ganegoda.

The Finance Ministry said yesterday that the CESS cuts on 800 import tariff lines under the 2027 Budget are meant to promote manufacturing, remove barriers to international trade and make Sri Lankan exports more competitive. It confirmed that the reductions under Budget Proposal No. 36.11 will take effect from 1 April, 2027, as published in Extraordinary Gazette No. 2479/38 on 10 March, 2026.

The phase-out began under 2023 Budget Proposal No. 34.6, which aimed to promote manufacturing industries and help domestic industries and enterprises, including agriculture, to grow. The 2025 Budget extended it with the aim of “presenting the import tariff structure on a rational basis, increasing export competitiveness and enhancing transparency in the tariff mechanism,” the Ministry said. CESS on 1,523 consumption goods lines is due to be removed in 2029.

The Daily FT reported on 14 November that CESS will go entirely on 499 lines from 1 April, 2027, and that all the listed lines will be cess-free by 1 April, 2029 (See https://www.ft.lk/front-page/CESS-cut-on-795-import-lines-from-April-2027/44-800095).

title: GEW Sri Lanka 2026 aims to expand opportunities for entrepreneurs nationwide | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 18 November 2026 00:00
-     - 33

Digital Economy Deputy Minister Eng. Eranga Weeraratne (second from left) speaks at the panel. Others from left: MayaHive Co-Founder LMS, AI and SaaS Consultant Sanjaya Elvitigala (Moderator), NGage Strategic Alliance Managing Director Sheron Jayasundara, Global Entrepreneurship Network National Ambassador for Sri Lanka and  Lanka Fishing Flies Managing DirectorSuresh de Mel and Kapruka Holdings Founder and Chairman Dulith Herath

By Safna Malik

Global Entrepreneurship Week (GEW) Sri Lanka 2026 was launched with a renewed focus on strengthening the country's entrepreneurial ecosystem, bringing together aspiring entrepreneurs, startups, small and medium enterprises (SMEs), business leaders and innovators to explore new pathways for growth and innovation.

Organised by the Global Entrepreneurship Network (GEN Global) in collaboration with the Ministry of Digital Economy, the Ministry of Industries and Entrepreneurship Development and the Ministry of Science and Technology, the initiative aims to connect entrepreneurs, businesses and ecosystem stakeholders across all 25 districts. The launch took place during Science Week, with the national campaign set to commence symbolically during Global Entrepreneurship Week from 16 to 22 November before continuing throughout the year through workshops, networking sessions, business exhibitions and entrepreneurship-focused events.

A key feature of the initiative will be the Entrepreneurship Marathon, which will bring together government institutions, private-sector organisations, academia, ecosystem enablers and bilateral and multilateral organisations to help entrepreneurs develop and scale their businesses.

Digital Economy Deputy Minister Eng. Eranga Weeraratne said entrepreneurship would play an important role in Sri Lanka's economic development, particularly in transforming innovation into products and services capable of reaching international markets.

“Entrepreneurship is vital to Sri Lanka's economic development, and we need entrepreneurs who can transform innovative ideas into products and services, access global markets and generate foreign exchange,” he said.

Weeraratne noted that Sri Lanka had secured fourth place globally for its implementation of Global Entrepreneurship Week initiatives and said the program provides opportunities for students, innovators and entrepreneurs to access knowledge, guidance and local and international business networks.

GEW Sri Lanka 2026 Program Director Charith Kandamulla said organisers hope to build on the momentum generated over the past year and expand support for entrepreneurs nationwide. “In 2025, we conducted 1,864 events nationwide, and GEN Global ranked Sri Lanka fourth among more than 200 countries for its active engagement in entrepreneurship. This year, we aim to build on these achievements by delivering 2,500 events, engaging 100,000 participants and supporting 5,000 entrepreneurs,” he said.

He added that the Entrepreneurship Marathon would serve as a platform for stronger collaboration across the entrepreneurial ecosystem, helping local businesses access the support, networks and opportunities required to grow.

Industry and Entrepreneurship Development Deputy Minister Chathuranga Abeysinghe stressed the need for stronger policy support to nurture entrepreneurship and innovation. “Entrepreneurship is a key requirement. We must recognise it, categorise it, and develop the policy framework necessary to build an ecosystem that enables it to move forward,” he said.

A panel discussion held alongside the launch explored the opportunities and challenges facing entrepreneurs in an increasingly digital and globally connected economy. The discussion featured Digital Economy Deputy Minister Eng. Eranga Weeraratne, Global Entrepreneurship Network National Ambassador for Sri Lanka and Managing Director of Lanka Fishing Flies Suresh de Mel, Kapruka Holdings PLC Founder and Chairman Dulith Herath, and NGage Strategic Alliance CEO Sheron Jayasundara.

How can innovators turn research into successful businesses?

Addressing the challenge of commercialising innovation, Weeraratne said many promising ideas struggle to progress beyond the research stage because founders often focus on technology rather than market demand. He stressed the importance of shifting from an engineering mindset towards building products that solve clearly defined problems and create value for customers.

According to Weeraratne, entrepreneurs must understand the markets they are targeting, develop multidisciplinary teams and think beyond local opportunities if they hope to attract investment and compete internationally. He warned that competing solely on price is rarely enough for long-term success and encouraged founders to identify gaps in existing industries where they can deliver something distinctive. “First, identify the problem you are going to solve. Then identify the resources you need to solve it.”

He added that innovators must also consider how they will access customers, investors and strategic partners as they move from concept to commercialisation.

What should entrepreneurs preserve as brands evolve?

Discussing branding in an era shaped by digital platforms and artificial intelligence, Jayasundara said the channels used to communicate with customers may have changed dramatically, but the foundations of strong brands remain the same.

She argued that credibility, trust and consistency continue to be the most valuable assets a business can build. While technologies evolve, successful brands are those that remain clear about who they are and what purpose they serve.

Jayasundara noted that businesses must continue communicating a consistent story while adapting to changing consumer expectations and technological shifts.

“Embrace the changes around your brand, but remain clear about its identity, its personality, and the need it fulfils.”

She said this clarity enables entrepreneurs to respond to new opportunities while maintaining the trust they have built with customers.

What does it take to build an export-oriented business?

Reflecting on his own entrepreneurial journey, de Mel spoke about the importance of understanding both products and markets before pursuing growth opportunities.

He explained how entering the fishing-flies business required learning about customers, supply chains, international markets and industry trends. That process, combined with active engagement in business organisations and industry networks, provided valuable knowledge and confidence as the company expanded.

De Mel said one of the most important decisions made during the company's growth journey was moving away from competing primarily on price and instead focusing on specialised, higher-value products capable of serving niche markets.

“Never give up, and build relationships with the partners in your ecosystem. Networking was key for me.”

He encouraged entrepreneurs to seek guidance, build relationships and learn from others rather than trying to navigate business challenges alone.

How is AI changing the way entrepreneurs build businesses?

Looking at the impact of artificial intelligence, Herath said today's entrepreneurs have advantages that previous generations did not enjoy.

He argued that AI-powered tools have lowered barriers to entry, reduced costs and made it easier for entrepreneurs to test ideas, launch products and learn from failures more quickly than before. “The cost of failure is much lower now. You can afford to experiment, fail, and try again.”

Herath noted that many of the capabilities that once required significant resources are now readily accessible through digital tools, making entrepreneurship more accessible to aspiring founders.

What support do startups need to grow internationally?

Turning to the broader startup ecosystem, Weeraratne said Sri Lanka needs policies and institutional support mechanisms that make it easier for startups to scale and attract investment.

He highlighted the importance of improving access to investors, strengthening innovation frameworks and creating pathways for startups to secure their first major customers.

“Funding is important, but so is the value investors can bring through market access and connections.”

Weeraratne also pointed to ongoing discussions around procurement reforms, innovation-focused investment mechanisms and greater access to data, which could help entrepreneurs develop and demonstrate new products and services.

How should startups communicate their value?

Jayasundara said entrepreneurs often make the mistake of focusing on their product before fully understanding the problem they are trying to solve.

She argued that effective communication begins with a clear understanding of customer needs and pain points. Rather than simply promoting a product, businesses should explain why it exists and how it addresses a specific customer challenge. “Here is the pain point, here is the problem, and here is my solution.”

According to Jayasundara, these considerations should form part of product development from the beginning rather than becoming an afterthought once a marketing campaign begins.

What should entrepreneurs consider before entering international markets?

Discussing international expansion, de Mel stressed the importance of market research, preparation and adaptability.

He noted that different markets often require different pricing strategies, product variations and approaches to customer engagement. Entrepreneurs must therefore invest time in understanding customer expectations and market conditions before pursuing growth overseas.

“It is very important to understand your market before entering it.”

He added that creativity, branding and product differentiation are increasingly important in helping businesses command stronger prices and compete effectively in crowded global markets.

How can AI create new opportunities for businesses?

Herath said artificial intelligence is also transforming how consumers discover businesses and products online.

As AI-powered search and recommendation tools become more widely used, entrepreneurs need to think about how their businesses are represented within these emerging digital ecosystems.

“Entrepreneurs should think about how their businesses can be represented in these new channels.”

He suggested that businesses that successfully adapt to new discovery mechanisms could benefit from increased visibility and access to new customers.

How can Sri Lanka prepare its workforce for an AI-driven future?

Looking ahead, Weeraratne said Sri Lanka must focus on both adopting new technologies and preparing people for the changes they will bring.

He noted that future workforce requirements will extend beyond technical expertise and include entrepreneurship, management and organisational change capabilities.

“We need people who can develop and implement solutions within organisations.”

According to Weeraratne, practical learning opportunities and industry exposure will be essential in helping individuals develop the skills required in an increasingly technology-driven economy.

How can startups compete with established brands?

Addressing competition, Jayasundara said startups should avoid trying to become smaller versions of already established brands.

Instead, entrepreneurs should identify underserved customer needs and market gaps where they can create meaningful differentiation and deliver greater value. “Learn from the leading brands, but find your own niche.”

She argued that smaller businesses often possess greater agility and can use closer customer relationships to develop solutions that larger organisations may overlook.

What should entrepreneurs keep in mind when expanding globally?

Returning to the subject of international growth, de Mel encouraged entrepreneurs to adopt a global mindset and make better use of available networks.

He said entrepreneurs should actively seek support from mentors, investors and ecosystem partners capable of helping them navigate unfamiliar markets and access new opportunities.

“Find your niche, then identify the stakeholders who can help you develop it.”

The ability to build relationships and remain connected to global entrepreneurial communities, he added, can significantly improve the prospects of long-term growth.

What role can digital public services play in entrepreneurship?

Weeraratne also outlined efforts to modernise public services and improve digital interactions between citizens, businesses and government institutions.

He said the objective is to reduce friction by enabling more services to be accessed online while creating opportunities for private-sector innovation through digital platforms and safe testing environments.

“The direction is towards connected platforms that allow institutions to make services available digitally.”

He added that more efficient digital services and payment systems could support broader economic participation and entrepreneurship.

Why does trust matter from day one?

Jayasundara highlights the importance of credibility and customer trust.

She said entrepreneurs themselves often become the face of their businesses, making reputation and customer relationships particularly important during the early stages of growth.

“Building trust and credibility is one of the most important things you can do.”

As customer feedback becomes increasingly visible through social media and digital platforms, he said businesses must be willing to listen, engage and respond constructively.

How can entrepreneurs make better use of networks?

Speaking on the importance of entrepreneurial networks, de Mel reiterated that building strong connections can play a critical role in business growth. He encouraged entrepreneurs to build their visibility, connect with peers locally and internationally, and remain open to learning from the experiences of others. “I have gained a great deal through networking and through the relationships I have built.”

As GEW Sri Lanka 2026 unfolds over the coming year, organisers hope the initiative will strengthen collaboration across the entrepreneurial ecosystem and help more Sri Lankans transform innovative ideas into sustainable businesses capable of competing on a global stage.

title: Policy sets direction. Who takes responsibility for implementing? | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 18 November 2026 00:25
-     - 74

Most who know me will know that much of my working life has been spent in senior corporate management, particularly in the tourism industry, setting business strategy, developing action plans and budgets, and leading operational teams responsible for carrying them through. We were responsible for delivering results, and explaining why something had not happened, and what course corrections we made to rectify the situation.

After retirement, for close upon seven years now, I have been working as a consultant to a leading development bank in Sri Lanka. This has required me to learn a different set of processes and appreciate the complexities of working with public institutions. In all honesty, it has not been easy, and some aspects still frustrate me. I do realise that the Government has responsibilities and constraints that a business does not, and it would be unreasonable to judge every public-sector decision by corporate standards. Even so, I find myself repeatedly asking what happens between agreeing on a desirable outcome and actually delivering it.

Over these years, my colleague and teammate, who is a trained professional in development, and I have had many discussions about public policy, its purpose and whether it ultimately achieves what it sets out to do, particularly in the Sri Lankan context. Those exchanges have made me question some of my own assumptions, but they have also sharpened my concern about the importance attached to formulating policies, compared with the effort devoted to implementing them.

So I am going to venture into unfamiliar waters and approach this subject from a management perspective. What follows is a reflection from someone whose working instincts were formed in corporate management and who is still trying to understand why an approved policy so often appears to receive more recognition than a result delivered.

Whenever a persistent problem is discussed in Sri Lanka, the conversation seems eventually to arrive at the need for a national policy. Sometimes there is already one available, in which case the answer is to revise it. The document is approved and launched with fanfare, yet the original problem can remain substantially unchanged, prompting yet another policy exercise a few years later.

Government needs an agreed direction that can outlast an individual minister. China’s successive five-year plans, for example, have kept industrial upgrading as a long-term priority while allowing the measures used to pursue it to change. In the United States, on the other hand, the federal clean vehicle tax credits expanded under Biden were brought to an early end under legislation signed by Trump in 2025.

The lesson for Sri Lanka, I think, is to seek broad agreement on a few long-term priorities and give them enough time to work, while remaining willing to change the approach when the evidence calls for it. My concern is where policy approval sits in the journey to achieving results. I have tried to make a comparison to illustrate the stages that I think must be followed in both the corporate and public sectors.

Figure 1  The delivery sequence in business and Government

From intention to delivery

In business, a strategic plan normally leads to an action plan, tested against available resources and translated into a budget. Responsibilities are assigned and performance reviewed.

Government has a more complicated task. It must reconcile competing interests (such as immigration/security giving opposing visa free options), respect legal rights and operate through multiple institutions with separate mandates. Cabinet approval does not automatically provide funding, amend legislation or give one ministry authority over another. These complications make a clear implementation plan more necessary. The sequence remains recognisable: policy direction, a delivery strategy, a budget action plan, funding and authorisations, assigned responsibility, execution and review.

Sri Lanka’s renewable electricity ambitions illustrate why a policy cannot be formulated in isolation from the arrangements needed to make it work. The target of generating 70% of our electricity from renewable sources by 2030 necessarily gives solar a substantial role. But expanding solar generation also requires timely investment in storage, stronger and stable networks and the controls needed to balance supply and demand. These requirements were recognised in electricity plans, yet grid readiness has not kept pace with solar expansion (CEB, 2025; PUCSL, 2026). Restrictions on additional grid-connected rooftop solar are now being introduced to manage the resulting constraints. Such limits may be necessary for immediate system security, but they raise an obvious management question of whether the supporting investments were funded, assigned and scheduled to arrive alongside the generation being encouraged?

Announcing the destination without organising the means of getting there is precisely the weakness that concerns me. If we were going to encourage solar generation on this scale, we should have planned, managed the roll out, and funded the work needed to accommodate it on the grid at the same time.

Regulations are one means of giving effect to policy. They can establish legally enforceable requirements, but they are not substitutes for operating capacity. A rule requiring proper waste disposal will achieve little where collection is unreliable, inspections are absent or enforcement is selective. A policy, a regulation and a functioning public service each perform a different task.

The appearance of reform

There is substantial research behind this concern. Matt Andrews, Lant Pritchett and Michael Woolcock, in their 2012 paper Escaping Capability Traps and their subsequent book Building State Capability, describe Governments adopting the outward appearance of effective institutions without acquiring their ability to perform.

They call this “isomorphic mimicry”. New structures, procedures and policy frameworks can demonstrate that reform is taking place, even when the service experienced by the public scarcely changes. (Andrews, Pritchett and Woolcock, 2012; 2017)

This may be a useful warning for Sri Lanka in the current context. A new framework may be necessary, but there is weak evidence of improvement. What matters is whether an approval becomes more predictable, a service more reliable or a public investment more useful.

An implementation plan on paper

The National Export Strategy received Cabinet approval in 2018 and was launched that July. It aimed to diversify exports and increase export revenue to US$28 billion by 2022. (Export Development Board, 2018a)

According to the Export Development Board’s own account, it identified actions, lead and supporting implementation partners, starting and finishing dates, tentative costs, checkpoints and milestones. It was explicitly designed to maintain continuity through political changes.

On 20 May 2024, after its 2018–2022 implementation period had ended, the Daily Mirror published “NES stuck in a NEST”. The commentary argued that ministries and institutional heads remained unaware of the documents and questioned who was responsible for advancing its logistics component. These are the writer of the article’s assessments, rather than findings of an independent implementation audit. (Daily Mirror, 2024)

Some implementation did occur: the Ministry’s 2024 progress report records EDB initiatives under NES priority sectors. The criticism therefore concerns incomplete and poorly coordinated delivery, rather than total inactivity. (Ministry of Industry and Entrepreneurship Development, 2024)

Take for example the recent budget proposals. It is reported that out of Rs. 1,380 billion allocated for capital projects in 2026, only about Rs. 385 billion (roughly 28%) was actually spent through September (EconomyNext)

Who will make it work

In Kishore Mahbubani’s 2024 memoir, Living the Asian Century,on Singapore’s development and in subsequent interviews around its publication, he attributes the success to the formula of meritocracy, pragmatism and honesty (MPH). He also applied these principles directly to Sri Lanka in an interview published on his website in October 202. [Mahbubani, 2024; Ilangamuwa, 2024]. He stated that Sri Lanka possessed the foundational potential to be even more successful than Singapore, but failed because it deviated from the core “MPH” formula.

Corruption affects which projects are chosen, who receives contracts and whose breaches are overlooked. Extending his principle to performance reporting, I would argue that institutions also need the freedom to acknowledge failure. A review cannot correct asprogram if everyone involved feels obliged to describe it as progressing satisfactorily, painting a rosy picture.

At the same time, we should resist turning Singapore into a simple formula for Sri Lanka. Its experience deserves study, but meritocracy, pragmatism and honesty do not automatically settle questions about public accountability, unequal opportunity or the rights of affected communities. Citizens must be able to question a decision even when its authors consider it efficient.

Bureaucracy is only part of the explanation

It is tempting to attribute the whole difficulty to bureaucracy. Excessive procedure, repeated referrals and reluctance to decide can certainly obstruct delivery. An official may be asked to carry out a commitment without sufficient funds or legal authority. A minister may support reform until it affects an influential constituency, while a transparent approval system may threaten those who benefit from discretion. In such circumstances, delay can reflect political resistance rather than administrative confusion.

The World Bank’s World Development Report 2017 makes this point. Policy effectiveness depends on credible commitments, coordination and cooperation, while unequal power and vested interests can undermine them. (World Bank, 2017)

Applied to our circumstances, it raises a question that receives too little attention at the launch of a policy: who is capable of carrying this through, and will that person have the authority to do so?

Implementation may require negotiation across agencies, procurement knowledge and the judgement to resolve problems as they arise. Even a capable official cannot deliver indefinitely without political support or control over essential resources.

A management team would be questioned about its inability to execute a business strategy and meet its agreed performance targets. The public sector needs equally serious attention to delivery capability, alongside the safeguards appropriate to public office. Its bureaucracy must be able to turn political intent into reliable administration.

Even competent public servants can spend much of their time securing routine clearances or sending the same file from one office to another. Yet a decision that has been held up for months can sometimes move in days when someone with political influence intervenes. There are safeguards that public administration must retain, but there is a problem when getting ordinary work done depends on who can pick up the phone. The task is to simplify procedures that serve little purpose and give officials the authority to make routine decisions, with clear accountability for how they use it.

We already have mechanisms in place

Sri Lanka does not lack institutions intended to monitor Government work. The Treasury’s Department of Project Management and Monitoring has responsibilities for reviewing major development initiatives, reporting performance and undertaking evaluations. Cabinet also approved arrangements in December 2023 for implementing the National Evaluation Policy from 2024, including a National Evaluation Steering Committee. (Department of Project Management and Monitoring, n.d.; Cabinet of Ministers, 2023)

The Auditor General and parliamentary committees provide further scrutiny. The relevant question is what happens after a weakness has been identified.

The IMF’s 2023 Governance Diagnostic uncovers an interesting finding. It noted requirements to identify remedial actions following Auditor General findings, but found no indication that the practices examined consistently included checking that those actions had occurred. (IMF, 2023). There are many examples.

Last year’s island-wide power-outage prompted inquiries, committees and reports. Recently there was another outage and investigations are again under way. The cause appears to be the same- unreliable sources of generation, an unstable grid with inadequate controls for safety. But the public is entitled to know what corrective measures were recommended after the earlier incident, which were implemented, and whether they worked as intended. Commissioning another inquiry cannot substitute for accounting for the findings of the previous one. It illustrates the distinction between reporting a problem and resolving it. A meeting can receive an explanation for a delay, record concern and request another report without changing the conditions causing the delay. Follow-up has value only when it produces a decision, assigns responsibility and establishes whether the correction was made.

What should count as progress

Taking another tourism example, Sri Lanka is now aiming to attract more high-spending tourists to increase yield. From a management perspective, my immediate question is what must happen to achieve this. Which visitor segments are we targeting, what experiences will persuade them to come, is the quality of the product and service in place, and can they justify the prices we hope to charge? These decisions must lead to specific work programs for product development, human resource training and marketing and promotions, with budgets, named responsibilities and deadlines. Progress would then be measured through changes in visitor spending, the earnings retained by local businesses and the quality of the visitor experience.

Publishing a policy, conducting workshops or launching a promotional campaign may contribute to that effort, but none, by itself, demonstrates that we have achieved higher yield. Someone must remain answerable for whether the intended result actually follows.

An implementation plan should therefore settle responsibility and resources early. It needs realistic costs, clarity about what depends on whom, and a way to resolve obstacles beyond the lead agency’s authority. This means involving the agencies, businesses and communities whose cooperation is needed while the plan is still being drawn up. They can identify practical difficulties and help establish what each can realistically contribute. That engagement should continue during implementation, with reviews examining whether the intended service or benefit is reaching people, alongside expenditure and schedules.

Officials should also need room to exercise judgement within clear rules. If a reasonable decision that fails attracts punishment while indefinite delay carries little consequence, ‘passing the file’ becomes an understandable response. Accountability should distinguish misconduct and neglect from an unsuccessful decision taken competently and in good faith.

Making somebody responsible for delivery

One practical response would be to require a clear delivery arrangement for every major policy. Where implementation crosses several ministries, a named programs director should lead a small dedicated team, with staff seconded for a defined period and their normal duties reassigned.  This is important for continuity, without having ad-hoc ministry officials participating at different meetings.

The team should have a clear action plan, with budgets and deliverables, delegated authority, deadlines and measurable outcomes. Funding must cover implementation and continuing operations. Holding someone responsible without giving them the authority and resources to act is hardly a credible management arrangement.

A small inter-ministerial steering committee, backed by an accountable political sponsor, should resolve obstacles beyond the team’s authority. Scheduled reviews must produce decisions, with corrective actions assigned to named individuals and completion dates. Progress should be measured against benefits delivered to the public, with independent verification where appropriate.

Every policy need not have a separate unit. Existing arrangements may suffice within one ministry, provided someone is clearly accountable. Dedicated teams should serve major priorities, with a defined handover to the institutions responsible for continuing operations. Otherwise, we risk creating another administrative layer that itself needs managing.

Evidence must inform the decision

There is also the question of whether the policy itself is sound.

Evidence-informed policymaking means examining the problem, comparing possible responses and using research, practical experience and evaluation to guide decisions (OECD, 2020). In tourism, the evidence available to do this varies considerably.

We may know how many visitors arrive in the country, yet not know  about what they spend in a particular destination, what are their primary needs or why they stay for shorter periods. Without that information, it is easy to prescribe more promotion when the real problem may be poor access or too little of the correct type of visitors. Sometimes the first step in making policy is to have good data and finding out what it really tells us.

Coming from corporate life, I would regard much of this as ordinary management discipline: establish why an intervention should work, test the assumptions and check the results. A capable team can execute a poorly conceived policy and still waste public money. Equally, excellent research cannot compensate for the absence of authority, funding or responsibility for delivery. We need both, with the willingness to change course when the results fail to support the original assumptions.

Conclusion

My reservation is about how enthusiastic we are to give credit for a policy. Formulating it is an achievement in its own right, but its value becomes clearer when we see what it changes for the people it is meant to serve.

Before commissioning a new policy, it would be useful to take stock of the previous one: what was put into practice, what difference it made, and where further work is needed. In my corporate years, such reviews often told us as much about what to keep as what to change. I think the same habit would serve the Government well. It would allow each new policy to build on what has already been learnt.

title: 2027 Budget: Navigating Sri Lanka’s pivot from stabilisation to transformation | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 18 November 2026 00:24
-     - 61

President and Finance Minister Anura Kumara Dissanayake presents 2027 Budget in 

Parliament last week

Introduction

Sri Lanka’s 2027 National Budget, presented on 12 November 2026, by President Anura Kumara Dissanayake in his capacity as of Finance, Planning and Economic Development, represents a decisive inflection point in the nation’s post-crisis economic trajectory. Framed explicitly as an intentional pivot “from economic stability towards transformation,” the Budget seeks to transition the economy from four years of painful austerity and macroeconomic stabilisation into a phase of high-velocity, investment-led expansion. Crucially, this shift occurs at a moment of profound institutional transition: the scheduled March 2027 conclusion of Sri Lanka’s four-year International Monetary Fund (IMF) Extended Fund Facility (EFF) program. Crafting a transformative Budget amidst lingering structural fragilities requires walking a macroeconomic tightrope. The

Government is launching an aggressive

Rs. 2 trillion public capital expenditure drive while simultaneously absorbing severe exogenous shocks—most notably the economic devastation of Cyclone Ditwah, which inflicted $ 3.4 billion in estimated damages, elevated global crude oil prices driven by Middle Eastern geopolitical conflict, and the looming threat of an El Niño peak in early 2027. For policymakers, international investors, and the broader public, the 2027 Budget is far more than an annual accounting exercise; it is a stress test of whether Sri Lanka has genuinely broken free from its historical cycle of twin deficits, debt distress, and policy slippage, or whether the post-IMF era risks reintroducing the very vulnerabilities that triggered the 2022 sovereign default.

The macroeconomic architecture: Balancing growth ambitions with fiscal guardrails

At the core of the 2027 Budget is an attempt to reconcile ambitious growth targets with the statutory discipline mandated by the Public Financial Management Act (PFMA) No. 44 of 2024. Building upon a 5.0% real GDP expansion in 2025 and 5.1% growth in the first quarter of 2026, the Government has set a bold medium-term growth trajectory exceeding 7.0%. To achieve this, total expenditure is projected at Rs. 7,673 billion (19.7% of GDP), rising to Rs. 7,933 billion (20.3% of GDP) once the Rs. 260 billion supplementary estimate for post-Cyclone Ditwah reconstruction is incorporated. On the revenue side, total revenue and grants are estimated at Rs. 6,180 billion (15.8% of GDP), with tax revenue accounting for 14.6% of GDP—moving steadily toward the medium-term statutory floor of 16%. Consequently, the headline Budget deficit is projected at 3.8% of GDP (Rs. 1,493 billion), widening to 4.5% of GDP (Rs. 1,753 billion) inclusive of disaster reconstruction. Crucially, this remains safely below the PFMA’s 5.0% legal ceiling, while the primary balance—the key metric of fiscal solvency—is projected at +2.3% of GDP (and +2.9%, or Rs. 1,150 billion, excluding Ditwah), aligning strictly with IMF program benchmarks. Macroeconomic Indicator2027 Target / Estimate Context and Policy Benchmarks Total Revenue and Grants Rs. 6,180 billion (15.8% of GDP)Tax revenue at 14.6% of GDP; medium-term floor set at 16%.Total expenditure: Rs. 7,673 billion (19.7% of GDP)Rises to Rs. 7,933 billion (20.3% of GDP) with Rs. 260 billion Ditwah allocation. Overall Budget Deficit3.8% of GDP (Rs. 1,493 billion) widens to 4.5% of GDP (Rs. 1,753B) with Ditwah; below 5% legal limit. Primary Balance+2.3% of GDP (incl. Ditwah)+2.9% (Rs. 1,150B) excluding Ditwah; meets IMF EFF targets. Public Investment (Capex) Rs. 2 trillion (5.12% of GDP). Exceeds the 4% medium-term floor to drive infrastructure and recovery. GDP Growth Trajectory: 7.0%+ (Medium-term target) follows 5.0% growth in 2025 and 5.1% in Q1 2026. However, beneath these compliant headline ratios lies a significant macroeconomic tension: the elasticity between real GDP growth and tax revenue buoyancy. The Budget simultaneously grants Rs. 28.4 billion in targeted tax relief—raising the Personal Income Tax (PIT) tax-free threshold from Rs. 1.8 million to Rs. 1.95 million annually, introducing a smoother 12% intermediate bracket, and lifting the threshold for the top 36% marginal rate, while attempting to broaden the base via capital gains taxes on cryptocurrencies, telecom licenses, and gems. If real economic growth tracks closer to the World Bank’s October 2026 projection of 4.2%–4.4% rather than the Government’s 7%+ aspiration, tax collections will inevitably underperform. Because interest payments alone consume roughly 43% of total Government revenue (Rs. 2,643 billion) alongside rigid public wages and Aswesuma welfare transfers, any revenue shortfall will force immediate, pro-cyclical cuts to capital expenditure—undermining the very engine required to reach higher growth.

The Rs. 2 t capital push and supply-side transformation

Unlike previous eras in which Sri Lankan public investment was frequently misallocated toward low-return, debt-funded vanity infrastructure, the 2027 Budget channels its Rs. 2 trillion (5.12% of GDP) capital expenditure allocation toward dismantling structural supply-side bottlenecks. A centrepiece of this strategy is energy transition and national grid resilience. Grid-scale Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) are slated to expand from 160 MW to 560 MW in 2027 (en route to 1,245 MW by 2029), backed by Rs. 26.5 billion for grid stabilisation. This is paired with a 500 MW floating solar initiative, a Rs. 3.5 billion household solar battery subsidy (Rs. 25,000 per kW up to Rs. 250,000), and the abolition of the 10% Ports and Airports Development Levy (PAL) on solar batteries. Simultaneously, the Budget allocates Rs. 251 billion to transport and connectivity, including an initial Rs. 80 billion to launch a multi-year railway electrification program, alongside Rs. 67.7 billion in state interest subsidies designed to unlock Rs. 174 billion in concessional credit for SMEs, paddy millers, fisheries exporters, and rural enterprises hiring Aswesuma recipients. Forward-looking modernisation initiatives, such as an AI Excellence Center, electricity tariff concessions for data centres, and Rs. 10,000 stock market portfolios for selected Advanced Level students to address the Colombo Stock Exchange’s abysmal 0.7% adult retail participation, signal a welcome focus on productivity and capital market deepening. Yet policymakers must confront a persistent institutional flaw: Sri Lanka’s historical inability to execute large capital Budgets efficiently. Chronic procurement bottlenecks, land acquisition delays, and bureaucratic inertia routinely depress capital Budget utilisation rates. Conversely, if the state manages to disburse the full Rs. 2 trillion rapidly without commensurate productivity gains or private-sector crowding-in, the sheer fiscal impulse risks overheating domestic demand, stoking inflation, which already spiked to 8.3% in October 2026 due to global fuel shocks and widening the fiscal deficit beyond sustainable bounds.

SOE reform and monetary policy coordination

Fiscal sustainability in Sri Lanka has historically been undermined by quasi-fiscal losses generated by State-Owned Enterprises (SOEs). The 2027 Budget builds upon a remarkable turnaround across 52 key SOEs, which shifted from a catastrophic aggregate loss of Rs. 774.6 billion in 2022 to a pre-tax profit of Rs. 444.4 billion in 2025 through cost-reflective pricing and balance sheet restructuring. To prevent remaining loss-makers from eroding fiscal space, the Government has appointed an expert committee to restructure Sri Lankan Airlines—burdened by Rs. 528 billion in accumulated losses, while opening Mattala Rajapaksa International Airport to international investor proposals. Equally critical is the strict institutional firewall separating fiscal policy from monetary operations. Following the October 2026 inflation surge to 8.3%, the Budget reaffirms absolute adherence to the Central Bank of Sri Lanka’s (CBSL) statutory price-stability mandate under the Central Bank Act, explicitly ruling out monetary financing of the fiscal deficit. Maintaining cost-recovery energy pricing and central bank independence will be the ultimate litmus test of institutional maturity once IMF quarterly reviews conclude in March 2027.

Balance of Payments fragilities: The return of the Current Account deficit

President Dissanayake rightly identified the external sector as Sri Lanka’s primary macroeconomic vulnerability. While gross official reserves have been rebuilt past $ 7 billion and workers’ remittances are projected to exceed $ 9 billion in 2026, the current account swung back into a $ 420 million deficit during January–September 2026, a sharp reversal from the $ 1,853 million surplus recorded during the same period in 2025. This deterioration reflects both rebounding import demand and a surging fuel import bill that reached $ 4.49 billion through September 2026. To bolster external competitiveness, the 2027 Budget introduces targeted trade and export facilitation measures: Input Cost Reduction: A 25% reduction in CESS across 800 import tariff lines (forgoing Rs. 10 billion in revenue) to lower raw material and intermediate input costs for domestic manufacturers and exporters. Exporter Liquidity and Maritime Incentives: Newly VAT-registered exporters whose exports exceed 80% of turnover over a six-month window will qualify as “eligible exporters” for accelerated VAT refunds, easing working capital bottlenecks. Additionally, bunker fuel sold to international shipping is exempted from the Social Security Contribution Levy (SSCL) to enhance Colombo’s maritime hub competitiveness, paired with performance-based foreign exchange payouts for tourism operators. Trade and Investment Integration: Plans to expand the Free Trade Agreement (FTA) with India, explore an FTA with China, and operationalise the newly gazetted Public-Private Partnership (PPP) framework to attract non-debt-creating foreign direct investment (FDI). Despite these welcome reforms, a critical structural vulnerability persists. A Rs. 2 trillion infrastructure push combined with CESS reductions across 800 items is inherently import-intensive. Without an immediate, commensurate surge in merchandise exports, higher imports of capital machinery and intermediate goods will widen the trade deficit. Furthermore, relying on workers’ remittances and tourism to offset a chronic merchandise trade deficit masks underlying weaknesses in tradable-goods competitiveness, leaving the Sri Lankan rupee acutely exposed to global labour market slowdowns or geopolitical shocks.

Exogenous shocks: Navigating oil volatility and the 2027 El Niño

Macroeconomic planning in Sri Lanka can no longer treat climate and geopolitical volatility as tail risks; they are recurring structural realities. The 2027 Budget allocates Rs. 260 billion for post-Cyclone Ditwah
reconstruction and establishes a Rs. 5 billion contingency fund to mitigate the projected February 2027 El Niño peak.  However, policymakers must recognise how these exogenous shocks interact with the Balance of Payments. An El Niño drought directly curtails hydropower generation capacity, forcing the Ceylon Electricity Board to rely heavily on imported thermal fuels precisely when Middle Eastern geopolitical tensions are keeping global oil prices elevated. Simultaneously, agricultural disruptions from El Niño risk reducing domestic paddy and food crop yields, necessitating emergency food imports that place dual pressure on headline inflation and CBSL foreign exchange reserves.

Debt sustainability and the 2028 repayment step-up

Sri Lanka’s debt metrics have improved substantially since the 2022 sovereign default. Central Government debt declined from 114.2% of GDP in 2022 to 95.0% at the end of 2025, is projected at 92.9% in 2026 and, according to the IMF’s Sixth Review—is now on track to reach 87% of GDP by 2032, outperforming the original 95% benchmark. Operationalising the independent Public Debt Management Office (PDMO) provides a vital institutional anchor for professionalising liability management. Nevertheless, the external debt service schedule reveals a deceptive calm in 2027 followed by a steepening maturity wall: 2025 (Actual): $ 3,707 million2026 (Estimate): $ 3,591 million2027 (Projected): $2,986 million (a temporary trough providing fiscal breathing room) 2028 (Projected): $ 3,574 million (a $ 588 million jump as bilateral principal moratoriums expire). Crucially, 2028 marks the end of the bilateral principal moratorium negotiated during restructuring, meaning principal amortisations resume alongside coupon payments on restructured Macro-Linked Bonds (MLBs). Using 2027’s $ 2,986 million trough to fund domestic capital expansion without ring-fencing foreign exchange for the 2028 step-up and the subsequent 2030–2032 peak when IMF EFF principal repayments commence would be a grave strategic error. Furthermore, financing the Rs. 1,753 billion overall deficits predominantly through domestic markets (within a Rs. 3.8 trillion gross borrowing cap) risks keeping 10-year Treasury yields elevated around 10.65%–11.05%, crowding out private-sector credit. At the same time, while Fitch’s upgrade of Sri Lanka’s sovereign rating to ‘B-’ signals progress, re-entering international sovereign bond markets prematurely at ‘B-’ yields would lock in punitive borrowing costs, reintroducing the exact commercial debt-servicing dynamics that caused the 2022 collapse.

The post-IMF transition: Avoiding the institutional anchor cliff

Exiting the IMF Extended Fund Facility in March 2027 removes external quarterly conditionality and disbursement discipline. Historically, Sri Lanka has suffered from severe “reform fatigue” immediately following the conclusion of IMF programs, rapidly unwinding tax reforms, restoring energy subsidies, and reverting to populist fiscal expansion.  While the PFMA (No. 44 of 2024) establishes binding domestic rules—capping primary expenditure at 13% of GDP and mandating primary surpluses—laws are only as durable as the political will enforcing them. International rating agencies and bondholders will scrutinise whether the newly appointed presidential committee evaluating post-March 2027 options maintains strict, rules-based transparency. Any perceived slippage in cost-recovery utility pricing or primary surplus targets (+2.3% of GDP) will immediately widen Sri Lanka’s sovereign risk premium.

An integrated policy framework for external and fiscal resilience

To bridge the gap between the 2027 Budget’s transformative ambitions and its structural risks, policymakers must execute an integrated mitigation framework across three pillars: Accelerating Energy Import Substitution: Fast-tracking the 560 MW grid-scale BESS rollout and rooftop solar incentives is not merely an environmental goal; it is the single most effective Balance of Payments hedge available. Displacing imported thermal power permanently lowers Sri Lanka’s structural import floor. Enforcing Strict Project Appraisal and PPP Mobilisation: To prevent the Rs. 2 trillion capital program from inflating deficits or crowding out private credit, the PDMO and National Planning Department must subject all state-funded projects to rigorous cost-benefit screening while shifting capital-intensive transport and port projects onto the newly gazetted PPP framework. Flexible Exchange Rate Management: The Central Bank must resist any temptation to defend artificial exchange rate bands in the face of oil spikes or El Niño import surges. Allowing the rupee to adjust smoothly serves as the primary shock absorber protecting gross official reserves above the $ 7 billion threshold.

A sequenced 2027–2028 liability management strategy

Rather than passively awaiting the $ 588 million jump in external debt service in 2028, the Public Debt Management Office should execute a disciplined, four-phase liability management strategy: Phase 1 (Q1–Q2 2027) — Reserve Ring-Fencing: Establish an explicit Foreign Exchange Debt-Service Sinking Fund during the 2027 repayment trough ($ 2.98 billion), sterilising and ring-fencing excess CBSL net dollar purchases and multilateral Budget support rather than allowing reserves to be absorbed by import growth. Phase 2 (Q3–Q4 2027) — Concessional Pre-Funding and Climate Swaps: Pre-fund 30%–40% of the 2028 repayment spike using low-cost World Bank (IBRD/IDA) and Asian Development Bank (ADB) Policy-Based Guarantees (PBGs) and development policy operations. Concurrently, leverage post-Cyclone Ditwah climate vulnerability and renewable energy targets to negotiate bilateral Debt-for-Climate swaps that retire near-term maturities at a discount.  Phase 3 (Q1–Q2 2028) — Opportunistic Liability Operations: If restructured sovereign bonds trade below par, utilise sinking fund resources to execute targeted buybacks or switches, extending 2028–2029 amortisations into 2033+ tenors. Any fresh international bond issuance must be capped at a modest benchmark ($ 500 million–$ 750 million) and strictly contingent on achieving at least a ‘B’ credit rating and u global yields. Phase 4 (Q3–Q4 2028) — Macro-Linked Bond (MLB) Sterilisation: Because Sri Lanka’s restructured International Sovereign Bonds contain MLB features that trigger higher payouts if nominal USD GDP outperforms, the Treasury must automatically capture growth-driven tax buoyancy and convert it into FX reserves ahead of MLB test dates. Throughout all four phases, debt managers must enforce two non-negotiable guardrails: keeping annual foreign currency debt service strictly at or below the IMF Debt Sustainability Analysis ceiling of 4.5% of GDP, and prohibiting unhedged external borrowing for domestic rupee-generating projects.

Summary and conclusion

Sri Lanka’s 2027 National Budget is an audacious blueprint that seeks to pivot the nation from austerity-driven stabilisation to infrastructure-led economic transformation. By adhering to the Public Financial Management Act’s deficit and primary surplus guardrails, prioritising renewable energy storage and transport connectivity, and introducing targeted exporter incentives, the Budget lays a credible conceptual foundation for higher medium-term growth. Yet macroeconomic success is never guaranteed by Budget speeches alone; it is forged in execution. The convergence of a re-emerging current account deficit, volatile global oil markets, an impending El Niño shock, and the March 2027 exit from the IMF Extended Fund Facility leaves zero margin for policy complacency. Above all, the temporary trough in 2027 external debt service ($ 2.99 billion) must not lull policymakers into a false sense of security ahead of the 2028 repayment step-up ($ 3.57 billion) and the 2030–2032 IMF principal wall. If the Government pairs its Rs. 2 trillion investment push with ironclad fiscal discipline, aggressive export diversification, and proactive liability management by the Public Debt Management Office, 2027 will be remembered as the year Sri Lanka’s recovery became irreversible. If discipline falters once external oversight recedes, the nation risks reliving the very macroeconomic imbalances it fought so hard to overcome.

title: Can new investment promotion agency boost FDI beyond $ 2 b? | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 18 November 2026 00:22
-     - 71

The President's Budget 2027 announced a proposal to set up a new company dedicated to promoting investment is a welcome step. It is to be wholly-owned by the Treasury, staffed by professionals with private sector and international experience, and offer market-competitive salaries. A bit like ‘GovTech’ today, and similar to ‘InvestSL’ envisaged in the Economic Transformation Act (2024). 

The announcement is a timely recognition that the current arrangement has not served Sri Lanka well. Annual average FDI inflows have languished around $ 1.2 billion over the past decade, and in the last five years it barely even reached $ 1 billion a year (CBSL Macroeconomic Chart Pack, 14 January 2026). The Board of Investment has long been asked to be promoter of investment, regulator and facilitator of entry, approver of incentives, and landlord of zones all at once. An agency that must court investors while also policing them, and bound by public sector pay scales and procedures, inevitably struggles to compete with many of the more agile, specialised promotion agencies seen in the rest of Asia. 

 

‘Invest SL’ - a starting point

The Government can draw on earlier thinking to help fast-track the implementation of this Budget 2027 proposal, rather than starting from scratch. Chapter XIII of the Economic Transformation Act of 2024 provides for establishing a new entity called ‘Invest Sri Lanka’, a dedicated investment promotion company incorporated under the Companies Act. The Chapter sets out the details - Invest SL was to be governed by a small professional board and empowered to hire expertise at competitive market rates. Its mandate: identify investment opportunities, promote Sri Lanka as a destination, link investors with local partners, and facilitate the establishment, retention and expansion of investments. That design came out of nearly a year of deliberation on the problems that needed solving, a review of global evidence on what makes promotion agencies effective, and a study of how peer countries do it.

Getting the model right

Beyond the announcement, what will matter next is how the new agency is designed. Two questions deserve careful thought.

First, how will the agency attract the right people? Competitive pay is necessary but not sufficient. The roles must offer a good amount of autonomy and a chance to work on deals that matter, or the best candidates won’t be interested to come. Nor should it be assumed that “a private sector background” alone makes someone the right fit. Selling a country to investors is a distinct skill, needing people who understand both how investors decide and how Government works. The agency should also be open to hiring foreign nationals, including market specialists from the countries Sri Lanka most wants to attract investment from. They can bring networks, language and an insider's understanding of how firms there make decisions. I recall how our approach and messaging to a Japanese investor audience during an investment promotion mission to Tokyo was greatly enriched and refined because the BOI had an in-house Japanese national advisor stationed from JETRO at that time. 


Second, how will the agency use outside expertise without depending on it? When a new agency must show results quickly, the temptation is to fill gaps with consultants. Used well, they can add real value, especially at the start. But consultants must be hired with clear deliverables and responsibility for outcomes. Their contracts can be tied to measurable results, such as qualified investor leads or projects that progress to commitment, and come with an explicit mandate to transfer skills to permanent staff. Above all, the core work cannot be outsourced: ‘learning’ must be an explicit objective. Sector knowledge, investor relationships and institutional memory must be steadily built in-house and retained – dependence on consultants must steadily fade.

Lost between interest and investment

A new, dedicated investment promotion agency is a necessary adjustment to the institutional architecture to drive FDI, but not a sufficient one on its own. An investor's interest converts to actual investment in the country only after land has been allocated, incentives are clarified, approvals have been granted, and operations begin. That is where Sri Lanka has too often lost investors. A recent Auditor General's report was quite revealing, in that regard (as reported in The Morning newspaper of 15 November 2026).

According to the report, of the $ 12.5 billion in investment committed under BOI agreements between 2015 and 2024, only $ 5.2 billion (around 41%) had materialised by the end of 2025. Of the 117 projects the BOI approved in 2025, only 65 went on to sign agreements. Some approvals have dragged on for up to three years. A capable investment promotion that generates strong leads could easily fall flat if the conversion stage is this slow, fragmented, and unpredictable. The appointment of a new Officials Committee on Land Allocation can help ease some of these issues.

Part of a broader reform

This is why the Economic Transformation Act did not stop at a promotions agency. It envisaged Invest SL as one part of a wider institutional overhaul, working alongside a high-powered Economic Commission that would replace the Board of Investment and take charge of facilitating investment, from approvals and incentives to coordinating across Government. Such a holistic reform is needed to avoid this new promotional agency becoming a well-paid front office for a back office that cannot deliver results.

Equally, investment promotion cannot sit apart from strategic thinking on which sectors will transform the economy. The ETA of 2024 recognised this. It tasked the Economic Commission with formulating national investment and trade policy together (section 32), determining investments that are of strategic importance (section 12), and ensuring that trade negotiations are aligned with the country's strategic export and investment objectives (section 14).

Time for greater ambition

Sri Lanka is on a stronger macroeconomic footing today, and averages of FDI inflows in the recent past need not be an indication of future prospects. A new agency can help lift FDI well beyond the current $ 1.2 billion average, to $ 2 billion and beyond, but only if promotion and facilitation are fixed together, and promotion is linked to larger strategic economic goals.

The proposed new agency's targeting must be closely linked to export development plans, and in sync with Sri Lanka's trade policy, especially the offensive and defensive interests carved out in new free trade agreements. Such joined-up thinking is what ensures investors are pursued in a targeted way, in sectors that diversify the economy, expand exports, bring technology spillovers and connect Sri Lankan firms to global capabilities and global supply chains.

(The author is Co-founder/Director of Centre for a Smart Future (CSF), and has advised on trade and investment strategies for countries in Asia, Africa, and the Caribbean. The author welcomes feedback on the article: connect@csf-asia.org)

title: Budget 2027 gives Sri Lanka’s exporters room to grow: An exporters perspective  | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 18 November 2026 00:21
-     - 84

For a Sri Lankan manufacturer, winning a first overseas order can take months. Missing the vessel by a day can undo much of that work. Having spent much of my career in export manufacturing, I read the 2027 Budget, presented by President Anura Kumara Dissanayake on 12 November, with that reality in mind. Can it help more Sri Lankan businesses win orders, produce at a competitive cost and deliver on time?

The President and the Government deserve credit for addressing several of the practical constraints that determine whether an exporter can do all three. The proposals on trade facilitation, VAT eligibility and investment in manufacturing are especially welcome. Their value will be measured in time saved, cash released for production and new orders won.

Making it easier to ship from Sri Lanka

The National Single Window for Trade is one of the Budget’s most practical reforms. A pilot for selected exports began on 5 November. The Government plans to bring exporters onto the system in the first half of 2027, followed by imports and re-exports in the second half, with nearly Rs. 2 billion allocated for the rollout. A single point of submission can reduce the time businesses spend sending the same information to several agencies. For a small exporter with a shipment deadline, being able to see where an application stands is valuable in itself. 

The proposal to modernise the Temporary Importation for Export Processing scheme deserves attention for similar reasons. Many local manufacturers need specialised inputs from abroad to produce finished goods here. Simpler access to those inputs under the scheme’s tax concessions can help smaller firms take on export orders that would otherwise stretch their resources.

Freeing up cash and encouraging investment

The Budget proposes that newly VAT-registered businesses qualify as eligible exporters if more than 80% of their turnover in the preceding six months comes from exports. This gives newer firms an earlier route to eligibility. It is a sensible change. A company can have a full order book and still struggle to buy materials or pay wages for its next production run while waiting for a VAT refund. Clear processing timelines and prompt refunds would give the proposal its full value. 

For manufacturers considering a larger investment, the Budget proposes a capital allowance equal to 200% of qualifying expenditure for eligible projects approved by the Board of Investment. Export manufacturers would need to invest at least US$3 million within three years. Alongside the Rs. 4 billion allocated for work on new and existing industrial estates, this can support decisions to install new machinery, expand production and bring more local suppliers into export supply chains.

Turning market access into orders

The Budget’s Rs. 750 million allocation covers Sri Lanka Expo 2027, planned for January, and priorities under the National Export Development Plan. A well-organised exhibition can give a small firm access to buyers it might spend months trying to reach. The commercial value comes afterwards, when a buyer requests samples, agrees on specifications and places an order. The EU-supported sustainable trade project can complement that work by helping businesses meet buyer requirements on testing, traceability and certification. 

The Government’s efforts to widen market access are also welcome. The Budget outlines work to expand the existing trade agreement with India, Sri Lanka’s application to join the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, and prospective agreements with the United Arab Emirates and Oman. To use any new trading terms, an exporter needs clear answers about tariffs, product standards and the documents required to qualify. 

From Nairobi, I see scope for Sri Lankan businesses to explore opportunities in East Africa in areas such as processed foods, rubber products, electrical goods and professional services. Finding the right partner is often the first commercial hurdle. An electrical goods manufacturer may need a distributor that can provide after-sales service. A food producer may need to adapt its packaging or labelling. Sri Lanka’s overseas missions and export promotion agencies can help firms assess demand and make those introductions before they commit significant time and money.

I also welcome the Government’s commitment to fiscal discipline. An exporter quoting today for delivery several months from now has to estimate the cost of materials, wages, freight and finance well before the buyer pays. Greater economic predictability gives businesses more confidence to make those commitments. 

The Government has chosen several reforms that can make a difference on the factory floor and at the port. A year from now, I would judge progress by three practical questions. Are shipments clearing faster? Are eligible firms receiving their VAT refunds sooner? And are more small manufacturers turning a first overseas order into repeat business? That second order is one of the clearest signs that a buyer trusts what Sri Lanka can deliver.

(The author is Sri Lanka’s High Commissioner to Kenya and a former Chairman of the Free Trade Zone Manufacturers’ Association. He writes in a personal capacity).

title: 2027 Budget: Can the financial sector turn policy ambitions into economic growth? | Daily FT
summary:
