Sri Lanka’s 2027 Budget places considerable emphasis on investment, enterprise development, exports and the revival of the rural economy. Yet, behind many of these ambitions lies an institution whose contribution could determine whether the proposals translate into meaningful economic outcomes by the financial sector.

The banking and financial system is expected to play a much wider role than simply providing loans. It must mobilise domestic savings, direct capital towards productive activities, support businesses, facilitate international trade, manage financial risks and help channel private investment into the economy.

One of the most significant financial-sector initiatives in the Budget is the allocation of Rs. 67.687 billion for interest subsidies and refinancing, with the expectation of generating approximately Rs. 174 billion in concessionary lending through State and private banks.

This represents a substantial intervention in the credit market. The Government reported that the Rs. 54.136 billion allocated for similar purposes in 2026 supported Rs. 97.1 billion in lending. The higher target for 2027 therefore signals an intention to use the banking system more aggressively as an instrument of economic recovery and transformation.

However, the central question is not simply how much money banks will lend. It is whether that financing will create additional productive capacity, strengthen businesses, generate employment and improve the country’s foreign-exchange earnings.

Credit as an instrument of economic transformation

The proposed concessionary lending programs cover a broad range of economic activities. These include the Re-MSME Plus program, additional financing for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises, loans for paddy millers, financing for women-headed households, rural enterprises, fisheries entrepreneurs and small-scale tourism operators.

The interest rates proposed for selected programs are significantly below prevailing market lending rates. The average weighted rate on new SME lending was 13.17% in September 2026, according to the Budget Economic and Fiscal Position Report. Against this background, concessionary rates of 3, 4 or 5% could provide meaningful relief to businesses facing high financing costs.

For many small enterprises, access to finance remains a fundamental constraint. Businesses may have viable products, established markets and opportunities for expansion but lack sufficient collateral, financial records or the credit history required by conventional lending models.

Banks therefore need to move beyond an approach that relies excessively on fixed-asset collateral. Cash-flow-based lending, sector-specific credit assessment and the use of reliable digital transaction records could help identify viable businesses that remain outside the formal credit system.

The effectiveness of these programs will also depend on the quality of the lending process. Subsidised interest rates should not become a reason to relax credit assessment. Banks must continue to evaluate repayment capacity, business viability and the intended use of funds.

A successful program should ultimately produce stronger enterprises and healthier loan portfolios, rather than merely higher disbursement figures.

The export and foreign-exchange dimension

The role of banks becomes even more important when the Budget’s financing initiatives are considered against Sri Lanka’s external-sector position.

During January to September 2026, merchandise exports amounted to approximately $10.75 billion, while imports reached $18.67 billion, resulting in a trade deficit of around $7.91 billion. Although workers’ remittances increased to $6.87 billion, tourism earnings declined by 9.2% to $2.25 billion.

These figures underline the importance of directing credit towards activities that strengthen the country’s capacity to earn foreign exchange.

Banks can support this objective through pre-shipment and post-shipment finance, export receivables financing, documentary trade instruments, supply-chain finance and foreign-exchange risk management.

The fisheries sector, agro-processing, food manufacturing, high-value manufacturing, logistics and tourism-related businesses offer opportunities for financing that can contribute to export earnings or reduce dependence on imported products.

Nevertheless, import financing should not be treated as inherently unproductive. Machinery, technology and intermediate goods can increase domestic production and future export capacity. The critical distinction is whether borrowed funds contribute to sustainable economic value.

The banking sector should therefore assess the economic purpose of financing rather than simply categorising transactions as import-related or export-related.

Beyond banks: the wider financial system must participate

Although commercial banks are assigned a prominent role in the concessionary lending programs, Sri Lanka’s financial-sector contribution should not be confined to traditional bank lending.

Licensed finance companies and leasing institutions can provide financing for machinery, commercial vehicles, equipment, renewable-energy systems and other productive assets. These institutions can serve smaller businesses that may not always fit conventional banking products.

The insurance industry has an equally important role. Agricultural production, fisheries, tourism and infrastructure investment are exposed to weather-related events, natural disasters and business interruptions. Without appropriate insurance protection, a single adverse event can undermine borrowers’ repayment capacity and weaken financial institutions’ asset quality.

The Budget’s reference to public-private partnerships, including the proposed logistics centre at Colombo Port, also creates opportunities for project finance, infrastructure bonds, institutional investment and insurance services.

Commercial banks can arrange project financing and working capital, while insurers can manage construction and operational risks. Pension funds and other institutional investors could contribute longer-term capital through appropriately structured investment instruments.

A more diversified financial system would reduce excessive dependence on bank balance sheets and create additional sources of funding for long-term development.

Capital markets: an opportunity to reduce dependence on debt

The Budget’s proposed SME Listing Support Mechanism and the ‘A Share for Everyone’ initiative are positive steps towards broadening capital-market participation.

The Colombo Stock Exchange is expected to deploy Rs. 250 million, with a further Rs. 500 million proposed for these initiatives. The Budget Speech also notes that active stock-market traders represent only around 0.7% of the population above 18 years of age.

For growing businesses, equity capital can be an important alternative to borrowing. Unlike debt, equity financing does not impose fixed interest and principal repayment obligations. It can therefore provide a more suitable funding structure for businesses undertaking expansion or innovation with uncertain short-term cash flows.

However, encouraging SMEs to list requires more than financial incentives. Businesses need support in accounting, corporate governance, auditing, valuation, legal compliance and investor relations. Market liquidity and investor confidence are equally important.

The success of the initiative should consequently be measured not only by the number of companies listed, but also by the amount of new capital raised and the extent to which participating businesses become stronger and more transparent.

The financial-stability challenge

The Budget’s ambition to expand affordable credit must be considered alongside the prevailing macroeconomic environment.

The Fiscal Position Report records inflation of 8.3% in October 2026, while the Central Bank’s Overnight Policy Rate was increased by 100 basis points to 8.75% in May and maintained at that level in September. The average weighted new lending rate stood at 12.65% in September.

At the same time, private-sector credit expanded by 23.6% year-on-year by the end of September 2026, with outstanding credit reaching approximately Rs. 11.77 trillion.

This indicates that credit demand is already growing substantially. While that is encouraging for economic recovery, rapid credit expansion must be accompanied by strong underwriting, appropriate provisioning and effective portfolio monitoring.

There is also a potential tension between subsidised lending and the cost of funds. Banks must be confident that interest subsidies and refinancing arrangements will be funded and reimbursed on time. Otherwise, delayed payments could affect lending margins, liquidity planning and the willingness of institutions to participate.

Importantly, an interest subsidy should not automatically be interpreted as a Government guarantee against borrower default. The respective responsibilities of the Treasury and lending institutions must be clearly defined.

Another issue is the relationship between Government borrowing and private-sector financing. The Fiscal Position Report places gross public debt at approximately Rs. 32,977 billion at the end of June 2026. Treasury Bonds represented 83.8% of central government domestic debt at the end of August.

Banks remain important participants in the Government securities market. If public-sector financing requirements absorb a disproportionate share of available financial resources, the capacity to finance private investment could be constrained. Maintaining a sustainable balance between sovereign financing and productive private-sector credit will therefore remain important.

Important questions on implementation and transparency

Despite the breadth of the proposed concessionary lending initiatives, several aspects of the program architecture require greater clarity.

The Budget identifies an overall expectation of Rs. 174 billion in concessionary lending. However, the individual program amounts described in the Speech add up to approximately Rs. 140 billion based on the stated figures. A program-by-program reconciliation would help explain the difference, including any existing allocations, overlaps or additional financing components.

More importantly, the published proposals would benefit from a consolidated framework setting out borrower eligibility, participating institutions, lending conditions, subsidy reimbursement arrangements, credit-risk allocation and performance-reporting requirements.

The distinction between additional lending and the relabelling of ordinary bank lending is also important. Public funds should generate financing that would not otherwise have been available on comparable terms.

(The author has an academic background in finance, economics and applied statistics, holding a degree in Finance and Investments from the University of South Wales, an MA in Economics and a Postgraduate Diploma in Applied Statistics from the University of Colombo, and a BA in Economics from the University of Peradeniya. The author is also associated with the Association of Chartered Certified Accountants (ACCA), UK)

2027 Budget:

Performance should therefore be assessed through indicators such as new businesses financed, additional investment generated, jobs created and sustained, export earnings, productivity improvements, repayment performance and the fiscal cost of each program.

The Budget’s own emphasis on accountable institutions, outcome indicators, cash-flow plans and public transparency provides a useful basis for such monitoring.

The need for financial resilience is also highlighted by the estimated Rs. 1,022.5 billion required for Cyclone Ditwah recovery and reconstruction over three years, including an additional expenditure requirement of approximately Rs. 260 billion in 2027. Such events demonstrate why climate-risk assessment, insurance coverage, business continuity and disaster-resilient lending must become integral parts of financial-sector planning.

From lending targets to measurable economic outcomes

Sri Lanka’s financial sector now faces an opportunity to become a more active partner in national economic transformation. But this requires a shift in emphasis from the volume of credit disbursed to the economic value created through that credit.

The Government should establish a consolidated concessionary-credit framework, publish clear subsidy and risk-sharing arrangements, and introduce a common reporting mechanism covering participating financial institutions. Independent evaluations after 12 and 24 months would help establish whether the programs are delivering genuine additionality.

Banks, meanwhile, should strengthen sector-specific lending strategies, expand cash-flow-based financing, support export-oriented enterprises and maintain rigorous risk management. Finance companies, leasing institutions, insurers and capital-market participants should also be recognised as complementary sources of finance and risk protection.

Ultimately, the 2027 Budget will not succeed merely because banks achieve a Rs. 174 billion lending target. Its success will depend on whether that financing creates productive businesses, improves competitiveness, generates sustainable employment, strengthens foreign-exchange earnings and remains financially sound.

The financial sector is not simply a channel through which budgetary policies are implemented. It is a strategic component of the country’s economic infrastructure. The challenge is to ensure that public resources, private capital and financial-sector expertise work together to turn the Budget’s policy ambitions into durable economic progress.

title: FCCISL says Budget 2027 opens way for growth from districts and villages | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 18 November 2026 00:00

Illustration of opportunities for producers, entrepreneurs and workers

The Federation of Chambers of Commerce and Industry of Sri Lanka (FCCISL) in a statement welcomed Budget 2027’s focus on public investment and enterprise support. 

To turn those proposals into jobs and orders for local businesses, FCCISL calls for realistic project budgets, timely payments and early government intervention when delivery is at risk. District and Divisional Secretaries can help agencies and businesses resolve obstacles close to where projects are delivered.

Public investment that reaches the districts

Annex III of the Budget Speech presented on 12 November puts public investment at Rs. 1,750 billion, 18.2% above the revised 2026 estimate. A proposed Rs. 260 billion supplementary estimate for Cyclone Ditwah reconstruction includes Rs. 250 billion for public investment and Rs. 10 billion for recurrent spending. With that supplement, proposed public investment reaches Rs. 2,000 billion, 35.1% above the revised 2026 estimate. The Budget was presented at Second Reading.

The Citizens Budget shows that transport has the largest capital component among the themes shown below. For district suppliers and contractors, the next steps are the publication of project scopes, funding schedules and tender dates.

District and divisional secretaries can connect projects to local needs

FCCISL proposes that District Secretaries convene line agencies, local authorities and chambers to review project readiness and publish expected tender dates. Divisional Secretaries can flag land, access, water and utility constraints early. Chambers can identify firms with the skills and equipment to bid and help others prepare for prequalification.

Illustration of public investment reaching rural communities

The capital schedule includes Rs. 2.8 billion for the Ingiriya–Ratnapura section of the A008. District chambers can help firms assess demand for construction and logistics services as project scopes become clear.

Better rural infrastructure can lift incomes and production

The Citizens Budget groups agriculture, irrigation, livestock, plantations, fisheries and land under a Rs. 273 billion theme. The Rs. 123 billion agriculture subcategory includes Rs. 44 billion for fertiliser support and Rs. 1.5 billion for crop insurance. Irrigation and livestock account for Rs. 93 billion and Rs. 9.4 billion respectively within the broader theme. Rural businesses can add value through testing, cold storage, aggregation and processing, sized to seasonal supply and confirmed buyer demand. For example, if 100 farms each supply 20 litres of milk a day and 80% is collected and accepted, the processor receives 1,600 litres a day before downtime. Firms can test that assumption against seasonal volumes and chilling capacity.

Illustration of improved road access linking producers to markets

Education and skills for district employers

The Budget Speech provides Rs. 1.5 billion in 2027 towards modernising 25 technical colleges across 25 districts and Rs. 800 million towards University of Vocational Technology facilities. District employers can identify shortages in skilled trades, hospitality and digital operations and offer supervised placements.

Tourism and hospitality beyond major centres

The Budget proposes Rs. 300 million from tourism authority funds to review and strengthen the Southern Mist Triangle across Galle, Matara and Ratnapura. Accommodation providers, guides, food suppliers and transport operators can develop joint offerings around visitor demand, reliable utilities and conservation requirements.

Rebuilding capacity after repeated shocks

The Easter Sunday attacks, COVID-19, the economic crisis and changes in policy direction weakened many firms’ working capital, staffing and equipment capacity. Contractors and suppliers still face debt repayments and uneven receipts. Timely certification and payment can help viable firms finance mobilisation and retain skilled workers.

Finance for local businesses and jobs

The Budget Speech proposes Re-MSME Plus lending at 5% and rural enterprise lending at 4% up to Rs. 5 million. The Citizens Budget also lists working-capital loans for growers of 35 eligible crops, including paddy, at 5% up to Rs. 3 million. Participating lenders and agencies should publish eligibility, security requirements and decision timelines. Partial credit guarantees and lender-led restructuring can help viable firms facing collateral or repayment constraints.

A profitable order can still leave a business short of cash when wages, suppliers and instalments fall due before customers pay. Positive operating cash flow gives SMEs and entrepreneurs room to reinvest and hire. Firms should test collection periods and working-capital needs before committing to new orders.

District producers can reach more buyers

The Budget Speech sets out Rs. 1.99 billion for the National Single Window for Trade, with wider exporter onboarding planned for the first half of 2027 and importer and re-export onboarding later in the year. It sets out Rs. 100 million to establish the separate National Single Window for Investment, with consultancy bids under evaluation at the time of the speech. The investment window can help local and foreign investors navigate approvals. District offices can help firms identify the agencies responsible for land, permits, utilities and environmental clearances. The Budget Speech also provides Rs. 750 million for activities including Sri Lanka Expo 2027 and export development priorities, and Rs. 4 billion for industrial estate development, feasibility work and upgrades. Chambers can help suppliers prepare for buyer meetings by checking certification, pricing and fulfilment capacity.

Reforms to lower production and service costs

How public investment can lead to economic benefits

FCCISL appreciates the steps the Government has taken since assuming office to improve public systems and advance policy, regulatory and administrative reforms. The Federation welcomes Budget 2027 funding for digitisation and the institutions, policies and regulations that support it, as well as efforts to broaden the tax base and strengthen revenue administration. Legislative changes include the Inland Revenue (Amendment) Act, No. 2 of 2025, which revised personal income tax provisions, and the Sri Lanka Electricity (Amendment) Act, No. 14 of 2025, which amended the legal framework for electricity sector policy.

The reform agenda offers scope to lower energy and utility costs, review duties and levies, and streamline regulatory, procurement, approval and payment procedures. Redesigning and digitising those processes can cut duplicate submissions and speed up approvals and payments. Automation and appropriate use of AI can handle routine tasks, with officials accountable for decisions. Shorter approval times, reliable utilities and timely payments can free working capital, reduce idle time and lower unit costs. That gives firms more room to invest in skills and technology, improve productivity and compete for domestic and export orders.

FCCISL and its chamber and industry association networks stand ready to support implementation by identifying the procedures that add the most time and cost and sharing practical feedback with the responsible agencies.

Policy certainty for investors and citizens

Predictable tax and regulatory rules, transparent decisions and dependable safeguards can build investor confidence. Firms should factor customs duties, utility costs and approval lead times into project and export plans.

Investment in digitisation

The Citizens Budget identifies Rs. 19.53 billion under digitisation of government services, including Rs. 9.48 billion for digital government transformation, Rs. 970 million for digitising divisional secretariats and Rs. 610 million for government-service cybersecurity. Assisted access and published response times can help rural businesses use those services.

Seven FCCISL proposals can support regional delivery

FCCISL’s proposals cover GovData SL, public service transformation, national business recovery, B-READY regulatory reform, a Galle district pilot, Sri Lanka–New Zealand cooperation and a public–private consortium model. These priorities offer scope for cooperation on secure data sharing, enterprise recovery, dairy development and transparent project partnerships.

Evolving challenges and disruptions

Skills shortages, utility outages, climate hazards, global conflict and cyber incidents can disrupt deliveries. Before bidding, firms should assess whether they have the cash, staff, equipment and materials to meet realistic schedules.

FCCISL calls for rapid and sustained Government intervention to help distressed businesses resume operations. A standing mechanism could receive early notices, convene public clients, lenders and chambers, set decision deadlines and refer unresolved matters. Joint reviews and mediation can prevent disagreements from escalating.

Businesses should be able to seek early intervention even where binding agreements apply. Any extension, variation or other relief should follow applicable contracts, procurement rules and statutory approvals.

Budget facilitation and faster decisions

Public clients can prevent payment and contract disputes by clarifying responsibilities, certifying work promptly and referring unresolved matters through established channels.

FCCISL urges agencies to prepare workable estimates using current prices, realistic schedules and expected payment commitments. Risk-based contingencies and clear approval procedures can help projects absorb unforeseen cost and supply shocks. FCCISL proposes an additional contingency of 10% of the base project cost estimate for evolving risks, alongside the customary allowance for physical scope changes and variations. This provision would help agencies respond to unforeseen price volatility, climate disruption and supply interruptions, with use subject to applicable approvals.

FCCISL appreciates two years of budget dialogue, including the opportunity for district chamber leaders to present proposals at the Presidential Secretariat. The Federation welcomes the consideration given to its proposals and the inclusion of regional priorities in government programmes. 

FCCISL President Dr. Rohitha Silva and the State Affairs Committee, chaired by Ruwan De Silva, reaffirm their readiness to work with Government through district and sectoral chambers, associations and institutions. FCCISL calls for public institutions to make business revival, entrepreneurship development and enterprise growth explicit priorities in their service mandate. Clear requirements, predictable response times and coordinated support at district and divisional levels can help entrepreneurs start and expand businesses, sustain profitability and create jobs.

RAWALPINDI: In an action-packed first day of Test cricket at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium yesterday, Pakistan dominated proceedings in the second Test, with their pace attack ripping through the Sri Lankan batting line-up to bundle them out for a paltry 98 – the lowest ever total in a Test innings at this venue.


In reply Pakistan finished the day brought forward by bad light on 121-3 to lead by 23 runs going into the second day today.

Plenty of eyebrows were raised and remarks made when Pakistan won the toss and opted to bowl first on this surface, yet the home team seamers made that decision look inspired. They wreaked absolute havoc, giving the Sri Lankan batting lineup no chance whatsoever to bundle them out cheaply. Only two Sri Lankan batters reached double figures; skipper Kusal Mendis top-scored with 32, alongside Sonal Dinusha on 21. Pakistan needed just four bowlers to wrap up the innings, with Mohammad Abbas, Razaullah, and Aamer Jamal taking three wickets apiece, while Saqib Khan chipped in with one.

Pasindu Sooriyabandara chased a wide ball, Dinesh Chandimal squeezed an inside edge onto the pad and was caught at forward short leg. Kamindu Mendis was undone by one that stopped on him and Dhananjaya de Silva got one that nipped back in late and stayed low. Lahiru Udara edged one to slip and Kusal Mendis holed out to long leg. Sri Lanka limped to lunch at 85-6.

Pakistan didn’t give Sri Lanka a sniff with the bat after the lunch break, capturing the remaining four wickets for just 13 runs. With the Pakistani seamers tearing through the batting lineup, many would have expected Sri Lanka to hit back in the same fashion. But once again Sri Lanka’s pacies were all over the place with the ball in hand, and their fielding was equally sloppy.

Pakistan’s opening batters took full advantage, batting wonderfully to dispatch the new ball to all parts of the ground. They provided a solid platform putting on 80. Once the opening partnership was broken, Sri Lanka struck twice more to claw their way back into the contest.

Tayyab Arif fell for a well-made 46 off 96 balls (6 fours). Mohammad Thaha edged a catch behind the wicket off Prabath Jayasuriya and Babar Azam was undone by a nip-backer from Lahiru Kumara that sneaked through and sent his off stump spinning. Azan Awais held onto one end to remain unbeaten on 47 with nightwatchman Saqib Khan on 2.

Sri Lanka made one change bringing in left-arm spinner Jayasuriya for left-arm seamer Dilshan Madushanka and Pakistan also made one change seamer Aamer Jamal coming in for spin bowling all-rounder Arafat Minhas.

The first Test of the two-match series ended in a draw.

The intensity of the contest occasionally spilled over into rough challenges, forcing the referee to intervene and caution players to maintain discipline. There were several promising attacking moves and close-range opportunities at both ends, but neither side managed to capitalise until Pakistan broke the deadlock just before the interval. He responded in the best possible manner, keeping his composure and guiding his team to a convincing championship triumph, silencing many of his critics in the process.

Pakistan, despite putting up a spirited fight and taking the initiative in the first half, ultimately fell short of their ambition as India demonstrated their championship pedigree when it mattered most.

Sai Gopal Rathod produced a breathtaking display of power hitting as South Asia cruised to a nine-wicket victory over Europe in the inaugural Test Twenty tournament at the SSC grounds yesterday.

The young batsman smashed an unbeaten 109 off just 51 deliveries, peppering the boundary with 15 fours and six sixes, as South Asia overhauled Europe’s combined total of 292 with 6.3 overs to spare.

The victory was particularly satisfying for South Asia mentor Rajkumar Sharma, best known as Virat Kohli’s childhood coach, whose charges got the better of a European outfit mentored by former West Indies Captain Sir Clive Lloyd.

However, Rathod’s fireworks were only half the story. Under Test Twenty’s innovative format, the boys’ and girls’ teams contribute towards a single result, with their scores combined to determine the winner.

South Asia’s girls had earlier laid the foundation with a disciplined bowling performance that restricted Europe to 113 for six from their allotted 20 overs. Ananya Srivastava top scored for Europe with 28, while Suhani Sharma contributed 26. South Asia’s bowlers maintained a tight leash throughout, with Rajshri Yadav conceding just nine runs from her four overs. Tanvika Gupta was equally economical, giving away only 12 runs from three overs.

South Asia’s girls then posted 134 for seven, securing a valuable 21 run advantage. Lalithya M.C. remained unbeaten on 29, while Siya Chugh chipped in with 25.

Europe’s boys, however, refused to surrender without a fight. Kavin Neeraj Chaddha struck a brisk 56 off 35 balls, including six boundaries and three sixes, as Europe amassed 179 for nine. Anirudh Sharma contributed 24, while Shiv Ratna Shreyas added a rapid 21.

That left South Asia’s boys requiring 159 to complete the victory. Rathod made light work of the target. After Harshit Tiwar contributed 25, the centurion took charge, striking the ball to all corners of the SSC. An astonishing 96 of his 109 runs came in boundaries as Europe ran out of answers.

South Asia reached 159 for one in just 13.3 overs, with Rathod deservedly taking the Player of the Match honours.

The result provided another illustration of Test Twenty’s central concept, where performances by boys and girls carry equal weight towards the final outcome. South Asia will next meet Australasia on Wednesday as the inaugural tournament continues in Colombo.

Europe Girls 113-6 (20), Europe Boys 179-9 (20) lost to South Asia Girls 134-7 (20), South Asia Boys 159-1 (13.3) by nine wickets

title: Budget 2027 boost for tourism | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 18 November 2026 00:10
-     - 19

President and Finance Minister Anura Kumara Dissanayake presents the 2027 Budget in Parliament last week

Budget 2027 abolishes the Tourism Development Levy and offers a 200% capital allowance for large hotel investments. It also commits funds to airports, heritage sites and cruise terminals to revive a tourism sector that analysts say lost momentum this year. 

Analysts welcomed the measures but noted that the levy relief is small and that subsidised home-stays could squeeze established hotels.

“The diversity of Sri Lanka’s tourist attractions is the most important and strongest potential of the country’s tourism industry,” President and Finance Minister Anura Kumara Dissanayake said, presenting the Budget on 12 November. He said tourism earnings reached $ 2,245 million by September. He added that the World Economic Forum had named Sri Lanka 10th in the world among tourism economies showing the fastest progress.

Analysts’ data points to a softer year. Softlogic Stockbrokers said tourist arrivals fell 2% to 1.9 million in the first 10 months of 2026, and tourism earnings fell 9% in the first nine months.

The headline measure is the end of the Tourism Development Levy (TDL), charged on the turnover of tourism establishments, from 1 April, 2027. “With the aim of reducing the tax burden on the tourism industry, enhancing its competitiveness and ensuring sustainable financing for tourism development, it is proposed to abolish the Tourism Development Levy currently charged on the turnover of tourism establishments,” the President said. Until a new financing mechanism is set up, the Treasury will fund the Sri Lanka Tourism Development Authority (SLTDA) on request.

The Budget estimates that abolishing the levy will cost only Rs. 40 million in revenue a year. First Capital Research said this makes it direct but modest cost relief for hotel operators. “The Tourism Development Levy on the turnover of tourism establishments will be abolished from 1 April, 2027, directly lowering operating costs for hotel operators,” HNB Stockbrokers said. HNB rated consumer services positive, citing the levy’s removal and the enhanced capital allowances.

Board of Investment (BOI)-approved tourism projects with a minimum investment of $ 3 million can opt for an enhanced capital allowance of 200% of qualifying capital expenditure. This replaces the existing allowance regime. First Capital said the lower effective tax could support new hotel capacity and refurbishments. It noted that hotels must invest within five years to qualify.

Softlogic said the abolition of the levy and a review of betting and gaming taxes would directly lift margins at John Keells Holdings, which owns Cinnamon Hotels and City of Dreams, and at John Keells Hotels. It said the end of the turnover-based levy also improves margins at Aitken Spence Hotel Holdings, Asian Hotels and Properties and Trans Asia Hotels, while the 200% allowance supports new builds and refurbishments. With the Gambling Regulatory Authority now operating, the Budget proposes a full review of taxes, fees and charges on betting and gaming to remove double taxation. First Capital said this could support the integrated resort and casino segment.

Access is the second pillar. Airport and Aviation Services (Sri Lanka) Ltd., (AASL) has begun a Rs. 15 billion expansion to raise Bandaranaike International Airport (BIA) Terminal 1 capacity from 6 million to 9 million passengers. The terminal is already handling more than its design capacity, and the Budget forecasts that 16 million will be needed by 2032. Rs. 100 million is allocated for the passenger terminal and other facilities at Sigiriya Domestic Airport, and AASL will upgrade China Bay Airport in Trincomalee in 2027. The Up-Country railway line is expected to be restored to Badulla by mid-2027.

On the heritage front, historic buildings around Colombo Fort will be restored and developed as a tourism zone with $ 77 million of World Bank funding. First Capital said the zone could boost footfall and room demand for Colombo city hotels over the medium term. The Dutch forts in Jaffna, Mannar, Kalpitiya and Batticaloa will be promoted as tourism hubs under public-private partnerships (PPPs), using Rs. 240 million of underutilised SLTDA funds.

Rs. 500 million is allocated to start relocating Galle Prison under the Galle Heritage City Development Plan. In Anuradhapura, the Central Cultural Fund has allocated Rs. 1,076 million for 2027. The Budget adds Rs. 500 million towards an Urban Development Authority plan estimated at Rs. 8.2 billion. Rs. 2.7 billion goes to branding 10 towns as tourism-focused urban centres, and Rs. 5 billion to develop 19 more.

Cruise and marine tourism also receive support. A cruise passenger terminal will be established at the Port of Colombo, and Rs. 240 million of SLTDA funds will modernise passenger terminal facilities in Galle, Tangalle and Trincomalee. The Sri Lanka Tourism Promotion Bureau will deploy Rs. 500 million for concessionary loans to help tourism service providers buy boats and other marine equipment. First Capital said the cruise and marine measures could widen arrivals and spending in coastal regions.

The Budget also extends cheap credit to smaller operators. Home-stay owners can borrow up to Rs. 2 million at 3% to upgrade or start home-based tourist accommodation, with total lending of Rs. 7.5 billion expected. CT Smith cautioned that the scheme cuts both ways. “However, subsidised homestays could intensify competition and pressure established hotels’ occupancy and room rates,” it said.

Other measures target the visitor experience. Rs. 300 million of SLTDA funds will go to strengthening the Southern Mist Triangle project around the Sinharaja rainforest. A centralised online e-ticketing system for the main attractions will receive Rs. 35 million, on top of Rs. 133 million from the SLTDA. Rs. 500 million is allocated to develop hotel schools in Polonnaruwa and Pinnawala. The Tourist Police will be strengthened with multilingual officers, patrol units at major sites, a 24-hour emergency hotline and a mobile app.

For wildlife tourism, the Wildlife Fund will provide an estimated Rs. 5 billion in phases for a new elephant transit home in Polonnaruwa, and Rs. 700 million for a wildlife hospital in Anuradhapura. The Budget also proposes free dual citizenship for the spouses and children of applicants and for third-generation members of the Sri Lankan diaspora, under a “Global Sri Lankan Heritage Citizen” program.

CT Smith rated tourism positive. It said the airport upgrades improve growth prospects for the sector. First Capital said better access and new attractions could lift occupancy at regional properties and open PPP opportunities.

title: Thema Collection shines at 2026 Global Responsible Tourism Awards | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 18 November 2026 00:03
-     - 13

Thema Collection’s CEO/Director Chamin Wickramasinghe (centre) receives the award

Amba Yaalu Kandalama, the all-women-run hotel of Thema Collection, has been named the global winner of the Diversity, Equity and Inclusion Responsible Tourism Award at the 2026 Global Responsible Tourism Awards. 

The winners were announced in London on 2 November during the annual ICRT Global Summit. Another Thema Collection property, Wild Glamping Gal Oya, was also recognised as a global finalist in the Regenerative Tourism category. 

Thema Collection’s CEO/Director Chamin Wickramasinghe, received the awards on behalf of the group at the ceremony in London.

Amba Yaalu - Kandalama was one of six category winners selected from 34 global finalists across 24 countries, each of which had first won gold in one of six regional awards to qualify. The judges recognised Amba Yaalu for a hospitality model in which women hold every position, from management to maintenance, combining experiences inspired by Sri Lankan culture and nature with a business built on women’s leadership and economic participation. The global win follows earlier global recognition for the property: earlier this year, Amba Yaalu - Kandalama was named Gender Equality Champion of the Year 2026 presented by Equality in Tourism. 

Professor Harold Goodwin, chair of the judges and founder of ICRT Global, said: “Each of our 2026 global finalists is to be applauded for taking responsibility for the impacts of tourism, measuring that impact and demonstrating a real difference. We hope each one will inspire others to act.”

Thema Collection Chairman and Founder Chandra Wickramasinghe said: “When we first thought of Amba Yaalu, we wanted to create opportunities for women in an industry where their participation has remained very low. The idea was also close to my heart, as I was inspired by my mother. Today, Amba Yaalu has 92 women working across its operations, including in areas traditionally considered male-dominated. What makes me most proud is seeing women who began with little or no experience grow into confident professionals, take responsibility and become examples for other women in their communities. Having Amba Yaalu recognised at a global level is both a proud and humbling moment for all of us.”

CEO/Director Chamin Wickramasinghe said: “Winning Gold at the Global Responsible Tourism Awards is a great encouragement for all of us at Thema Collection. Amba Yaalu was started to give women more opportunities in our industry, and when we introduced the idea of an all-women-run hotel, there were challenges. We had to invest time in training, build confidence and give our team the trust and responsibility to manage the operation. Today, seeing how the women at Amba Yaalu have taken ownership of their work makes us very happy. I hope our experience will encourage other hotels and businesses in Sri Lanka to give more women the chance to build careers and take on leadership roles. I am also delighted to see Wild Glamping Gal Oya among the global finalists, and I thank our whole team.”

Thema Collection’s Wild Glamping Gal Oya was also named a global finalist in the Regenerative Tourism Responsible Tourism Award, having first won gold at regional level to qualify. The judges recognised how the property has transformed former cultivation land into an organic farming and low-impact tourism destination. Its wildlife and cultural experiences benefit local guides, farmers, artisans and the Rathugala Vedda community, and the judges praised its contribution to regenerating nature and livelihoods.

Silk Route Enterprises, with the support of the Government of Pakistan, organised the second edition of the Silk Route Festival 2026 in Islamabad from 24 to 25 October 2026, bringing together representatives of the diplomatic community, business sector, government institutions and the public to promote regional cooperation and cultural exchange.

The two-day festival featured panel discussions on collaboration in tourism, culture and people-to-people contacts, traditional cuisine showcases and visits to historical and heritage sites. The event provided a platform to strengthen regional ties, foster cultural understanding and promote tourism among participating countries.

At the invitation of the organisers, High Commissioner of Sri Lanka to Pakistan, Rear Admiral Fred Senevirathne, attended the plenary session as a Guest of Honour and participated as a panellist in the Pakistan Cultural Diplomacy Dialogue. Sri Lanka Tourism Development Authority Chairman Suranjith Wewita, and Deputy Director General Krishantha Bopage, also participated as keynote speakers. 

The Sri Lanka High Commission in Islamabad organised a dedicated Sri Lankan stall showcasing the country’s rich cultural and culinary heritage, along with video presentations and promotional materials highlighting its diverse tourism attractions and destinations. The stall attracted visitors and provided an opportunity to promote Sri Lanka as an attractive destination for tourism and cultural experiences.

The festival was attended by members of the diplomatic community, business representatives, senior government officials and other distinguished guests, providing opportunities for engagement, networking and closer regional cooperation.

Sri Lanka’s participation in the Silk Route Festival 2026 reaffirmed the commitment of the Sri Lanka High Commission to strengthening Sri Lanka-Pakistan relations and promoting tourism, cultural exchanges and people-to-people connections between the two countries.

title: Radisson hotels in SL simultaneously achieve premium highest level of Safehotels Certification | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 18 November 2026 00:00
-     - 9

Radisson Blu Resort Galle, Radisson Hotel Colombo, and Radisson Hotel Kandy have achieved the prestigious Safehotels Premium Level Certification, marking a significant milestone as all three properties attain the highest certification category offered by Safehotels for the first time together. Awarded by Safehotels Alliance AB, an internationally recognised hotel safety and security certification organisation established in Sweden, this achievement underscores the trio of hotels’ commitment to providing guests with safe, secure, and reassuring hospitality experiences.

Established in 2001, Safehotels provides independent safety and security certification for hotels worldwide, with a presence in over 70 countries and 175 cities. Its certification programme is designed to assess and verify hotel safety and security standards against the Safehotels Global Hotel Security Standard. The programme evaluates a property’s preparedness, operational procedures, and ability to maintain a secure environment for guests, employees, and visitors.

The certification process involves a comprehensive on site assessment conducted by experienced Safehotels auditors. This includes detailed property walkthroughs, visual inspections, face to face interviews with relevant management and team members, and the testing and inspection of selected fire safety and security systems and equipment. Hotels are also required to submit supporting documentation covering fire safety, security, and crisis management procedures, emergency plans, and relevant service records. Following the assessment, a detailed report identifies the certification outcome and any corrective actions required to meet the prescribed standards.

Achieving the Premium Level Certification demonstrates that all three Radisson properties have successfully met the rigorous assessment requirements, reflecting their commitment to maintaining effective safety and security practices across critical operational areas, including emergency preparedness, fire safety, crisis management, and overall hotel security. The certification is valid for one year, with annual reassessments ensuring that certified properties continue to uphold the required standards.

Cluster General Manager for the portfolio Kristofer Quadros said: “We have consistently maintained the Safehotels standards across our three properties, and achieving the highest Premium Level certification simultaneously at all three hotels marks a significant milestone for us. This accomplishment reflects the dedication and collective efforts of our teams in creating safe and secure environments for our guests, team members, and assets. We remain committed to continually strengthening our safety and security practices while delivering the exceptional hospitality experiences our guests expect from us.”

With this achievement, Radisson Blu Resort Galle, Radisson Hotel Colombo, and Radisson Hotel Kandy further reinforce their position as trusted hospitality destinations in Sri Lanka. The milestone highlights the Trio of Radisson hotels’ continued dedication to responsible hotel operations, internationally recognised safety standards, and guest wellbeing, ensuring that every stay is supported by the reassurance of a safe and secure environment.
